claims.claim: The specific work being displaced to pay for the deletionOrder feature is the Source Hydrator History & Rollback ticket: the dev pair that would have made the Rollback tab render to the sync branch is moved onto the progressive sync deletion loop and the rollback work slips a full quarter. That is the named cost of saying yes to the PRD, and nothing in the PRD's Drawbacks section ('Slight increase in Argo CD code base complexity') accounts for it.

Deprioritizing the rollback ticket and staffing the deletion loop buys a feature whose failure mode has no recovery path. The Reverse deletionOrder waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving to the next, so a stalled child halts the sequence with the ApplicationSet partially torn down; the only proposed mechanism for restoring a known-good rendered state is the checkout-old-rendered-manifests rollback in the very ticket that was deferred to next quarter. The two decisions were made on the same call and their interaction was not priced.

The PRD contradicts a commitment already on the roadmap. The roadmap states under First class support for ApplicationSet resources that 'ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented' and that 'Teardown remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time'; the PRD's stated goal is a Reverse deletionOrder that deletes ApplicationSet children in the reverse order of the RollingSync steps. Both cannot hold, and neither document cites the other.

No one is designated to settle the roadmap-versus-PRD contradiction, so it will be resolved by whoever merges first rather than by a decision. The PRD lists sponsors, reviewers and approvers all as TBD, and the incident review explicitly declined to decide ('needs an owner. not deciding here'). By contrast the impersonation RFC names three approvers, which shows the project does assign approvers when it intends a call to be made — the deletion PRD reverses a published roadmap line with that slot empty.

The agreed impersonation rollout shape is not the shape the RFC designed. The platform sync call decided impersonation 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide', while the RFC states as a goal that 'The feature can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications' and specifies the enablement surface as the argocd-cm key, the ARGOCD_APPLICATION_CONTROLLER_ENABLE_IMPERSONATION environment variable, and the --enable-impersonation flag — all controller-scoped. A per-project gate is unbuilt work that nobody costed when the decision was recorded as 'a real decision, not a maybe'.

The condition gating the impersonation rollout — 'nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed' — is held open by work no roadmap line funds. Fixing it means making Server-Side Diff honor destinationServiceAccounts on the diff path, since diff currently runs as the cluster Secret credential and server-side apply dry-run is authorized as patch, with no dry-run verb in Kubernetes RBAC. The roadmap's only multi-tenancy entries are Applications-outside-argocd-namespace and AppSource; nothing on record commits anyone to the diff identity work, so the gate has no scheduled end.

Enabling impersonation before the diff path is fixed converts a security improvement into an unbounded RBAC expansion, which is the opposite of the RFC's stated motivation of least privilege. The CI diff failures were root-caused to the diff running as the destination service account rather than the control plane identity; the external-cluster report shows the remedy teams actually reach for is adding another patch rule per new resource kind — five rounds so far with 'no end state' — because a ComparisonError forces the grant. Each round widens the standing cluster credential the RFC set out to narrow.

The evidence that ordered deletion is the wrong bet is already observable and predates the spend: the delete/recreate infinite loop reproduced in staging under the reverse deletion order, where the wait-for-full-deletion semantics never complete against an Application stuck Progressing and the controller restarts the wave from the top. The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section says 'No immediate Risks to consider' and its Security Considerations claim no impact because no additional privileges are needed — neither statement survives the reproduced defect.

The only thing standing between the reproduced wave-restart loop and production is an unenforced human habit. The incident runbook rule is to switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before deleting any child Application by hand, but the PRD ships deletionOrder as a spec field on ApplicationSetStrategy with no controller-level check tying it to hydrated repositories, where each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. Shipping the field without the check makes the mitigation depend on operators remembering a runbook line during an incident.

If the deletion bet succeeds completely, the next demand it unlocks points straight back at the line the roadmap says is closed. The ApplicationSet Source Hydrator request wants DAG-based Application destroy ordering across multiple ApplicationSets, which the PRD's per-ApplicationSet deletionOrder cannot express because it derives its order from that one ApplicationSet's own rollingSync steps. Success therefore produces pressure for cross-ApplicationSet teardown orchestration, and the roadmap's standing position is that ordered deletion of ApplicationSet children is out of scope for rollout orchestration entirely.

The ApplicationSet Source Hydrator request asks for precisely the combination the incident review prohibited. Its proposal has an ApplicationSet hydrate child Applications into a Git repo and enforce ordering through sync-waves, while the review's interim call is that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there is a debounce, because each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. Granting the request would either lift the prohibition or ship a feature its users are told not to combine with rollout ordering.

The Helm DrySource request asks the project to spend the opinion the hydrator RFC deliberately bought. The RFC rules out multiple sources referenced in the same application as nondeterministic external configuration, states that only one source may be the dry source, and recommends the umbrella chart approach instead of external values files; the ticket's stated blocker is exactly that using Helm dependencies is unworkable with ApplicationSets for cross-environment chart versions, and it further requires SyncSource and HydrateTo to point at different repositories. Saying yes costs the reproducibility guarantee that the RFC's preview and promotion rules rest on.

Promoting Progressive Sync to Stable would publish a maturity claim that current standing practice contradicts. Stable is defined as tested and validated with various use cases, yet one whole use case — progressive sync on hydrator pilot repositories — is under an active prohibition pending a debounce, and the pilot ticket records that every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit picked up as a source change. Stability declared while a named combination is operationally banned sets an expectation the feature cannot meet on upgrade.

The push-to-stage half of the hydrator rests on a component nobody owns. The RFC's push-to-stage mode explicitly 'relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch' and calls that the integration point for automated promotion; the platform sync call records that the stage-branch promoter is still a shell script with no owner, and parks it. The hydrator's staleness bug shows what that costs: in push-to-stage mode the external promoter has not yet moved fresh manifests, so auto-sync deploys whatever the stage branch last held.

Two open tickets describe the same underlying defect in the hydrator's push path without referencing each other: hydrated commits are pushed unsigned, so a branch with signature verification enabled rejects Argo CD's own output, and the RFC's own security section leaves the git permissions and push-secret story as an open consideration while specifying the repository-write Secret as the only control. The commit server the RFC delegates the push to is the same component the signing proposal would gate at startup, which makes signing a change to the RFC's unwritten security posture rather than an isolated feature flag.

The PRD's Non-Goals section commits to shipping a field that silently ignores valid-looking input: users setting the custom deletion strategy get a configuration field that accepts input with no UI statement that the option is unavailable. Combined with the PRD's own implementation note that a check must correlate deletionStrategy to the ApplicationSet strategy and error out when Reverse is selected without an ordered rollingSync, the design applies validation to one unsupported combination and deliberately withholds it from another, which is the harder failure to diagnose during a teardown.
